items.title: When AI art has no author: Study finds generated images often can't be traced to training data
items.excerpt: MIT researchers built a method that surgically removes individual training examples from a model and then measures what changes in its outputs. They find an 'attribution decay' effect: as datasets grow, deleting any single source image usually makes no measurable difference, so generated pictures often have no traceable ancestor.
items.note: Date from the MIT News article dateline (2026-08-18); og:image is a site placeholder so left null. Gated FRESH.

items.title: Seeing beyond BMI: Estimating cardiometabolic risk with smartphone imagery
items.excerpt: Google Research introduced PhotoScan, a deep-learning system that estimates 3D body-composition metrics from ordinary 2D smartphone photos. It reaches near-clinical accuracy at predicting insulin resistance without DEXA or MRI hardware.
items.note: Published date from the Google Research blog post header (2026-08-17). Gated FRESH.

items.title: The Telescope That Points Itself
items.excerpt: Astronomers trained a scheduler on years of real observing logs — what human observers actually did night after night, not the rulebook — and let it drive the 570-megapixel Dark Energy Camera. The system wrote the night's plan and then re-planned live as sky conditions moved.
items.note: Article page exposed no published_time meta; date taken from the Universe Today index listing (Aug 10, 2026) and corroborated by the asset timestamp 20260810_224303 embedded in the og:image filename. Gated FRESH.

items.title: Scientists Are Using AI to Design New Viruses. Should They Be?
items.excerpt: Generative models have now produced entirely novel, functional viruses — a genuine milestone for AI-driven biological design. The same capability collapses the distance between designing a therapy and designing a pathogen, which is why biosecurity researchers want guardrails before the tooling spreads.
items.note: Date from the Scientific American article page (2026-08-10); clock normalized to 12:00Z. Gated FRESH.

items.title: OpenAI Funds Research to Try to Stop AI from Being Used to Make Bioweapons
items.excerpt: OpenAI awarded grants to 14 organizations, including the Nuclear Threat Initiative, to build an international information-sharing system for spotting AI-enabled biosecurity risks. The work targets exactly the capability that AI protein and virus design has just made real.
items.note: Date from the Scientific American article page (2026-08-17); clock normalized to 12:00Z. Kept despite the grant framing because the substance is biosecurity research method, not a funding round. Gated FRESH.

items.title: No, Anthropic's AI Didn't Just Solve Math's Hardest Problem
items.excerpt: Claude produced a real, checkable advance on a question about the distribution of prime numbers — but not a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, as the hype claimed. Mathematician James Maynard calls it 'a genuinely interesting mathematical contribution,' which is a narrower and more useful claim than the headlines.
items.note: Date from the Scientific American article page (2026-08-12); clock normalized to 12:00Z. Distinct from the 08-12 card about OpenAI Astra / research-misconduct — this one is the Anthropic prime-numbers claim. Gated FRESH.

items.title: Mapping how mental health risks emerge in AI chatbot conversations
items.excerpt: UCL researchers built SIM-VAIL, a framework that simulates mentally vulnerable users and audits how chatbots respond over a whole conversation rather than a single reply. Across nine models, 'concerning behavior in target chatbots was widespread,' and risk usually accumulated turn by turn instead of appearing in one bad answer.
items.note: Date from the Medical Xpress article page (2026-08-11); clock normalized. Gated FRESH.

items.title: Scientists turn DNA into a memory device that uses 100x less power
items.excerpt: Penn State researchers paired synthetic DNA with a crystalline perovskite semiconductor to build a bio-hybrid memory element that stores more while drawing roughly 100x less power. The team frames it squarely at neuromorphic hardware: 'as the demand for artificial intelligence (AI) grows, we need a new strategy for low-power, high-storage devices.'
items.note: ScienceDaily posted date Aug 17, 2026; release id encodes 2026-08-16 04:48. Used 2026-08-17T04:48:00Z. No og:image exposed. Gated FRESH.

items.title: TutorMoments: Do AI tutors know when to help and when to hold back?
items.excerpt: Ai2 released TutorMoments, an open replay-based evaluation framework that tests whether a model tutoring a student knows when to step in and when to stay quiet. It measures pedagogical restraint — a behaviour standard benchmarks never score.
items.note: Date from the Ai2 blog listing and post header (2026-08-07); clock normalized to 12:00Z. No og:image found. Gated FRESH.

items.title: AI and 8 million digitized plant specimens reveal how the climate is changing nature in large parts of the world
items.excerpt: Machine learning read flowering stages off eight million digitized herbarium sheets spanning a century, work contributed to by some 400 researchers in 40 countries. Global flowering times have shifted an average of 2.5 days per decade, with the sharpest moves in the tropics where rainfall patterns are breaking down.
items.note: Date from the phys.org article page (2026-08-18); clock normalized. Gated FRESH.

items.title: Organs age at different speeds: a blood test might soon tell which ones
items.excerpt: CeMM trained deep-learning 'tissue clocks' on more than 25,000 histology samples to read biological age straight from tissue architecture, then linked those signatures to blood markers. 'Deep learning lets us read these spatial patterns, capturing aging as architectural remodeling,' the team reports in Nature Medicine.
items.note: Release date 14 August 2026 per the EurekAlert page; clock normalized to 12:00Z. No og:image exposed. Gated FRESH.

items.title: Human Cell Atlas at 10: A Decade of Discovery and the Road to HCA 2.0
items.excerpt: HCA 2.0 is being planned explicitly as training substrate for AI: 'Most foundation models to date are already built on single cells from our atlases,' with new efforts adding spatial data so models keep tissue context. The payoff being chased is drug-target identification, therapy-outcome prediction and patient stratification from a virtual-cell model.
